name: Kira Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can give me the public version and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy kitchenware and homeware for Brightwell Home Supplies, which sells to about 600 independent shops. Saucepans, storage tubs, glassware, that sort of thing, mostly from factories overseas. My day is half email with factory agents and half deciding what to stock for spring or Christmas. I like the hunt for a good product that nobody else has found, and I hate chasing late shipments at 7 a.m. because of the time difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because everyone's been shouting about it and I'd rather have a quiet life. I'd tell my friends in the choir that I use it for the odd email and that's about it. Online I'd keep out of it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel fine about work. My husband Joseph drives buses for the city and his job is stable, our mortgage is gone and the kids are independent. The only thing that nags is that Brightwell's owners keep bargaining us down on bonuses, with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, and keep using the chat tool to draft the awkward emails to factories and to translate spec sheets. That saves me maybe two hours a week. I'd retire at 62 as planned and spend more time at the allotment and singing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a relief, really. I'd feel I was left alone to do a job I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the bonus freeze. Is that something you'd still worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bonus freeze two years ago, and the staff were told it was 'market conditions'. Our union rep took it up, and we got half back. That's the sort of pressure I'd still be dealing with, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Joseph talk about over dinner in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joseph is a union rep too, so we talk about it over dinner. We both think that if the owners get richer, the workers should see some of it. Whatever the machines do for the owners, I want a fair share to reach the people who actually do the work.

say: I'd say it's **hype** and I'd keep out of the online noise.
I'd tell my choir friends I use it for the odd **email** and that's all.
think: Work feels fine, and the one nag is **bonuses** squeezed by the owners.
Our mortgage is paid, so we have real **breathing room**.
do: Keep using the chat tool to **draft** emails to factories and translate spec sheets.
Plan to **retire** at 62 as I'd always planned.
Spend more time at the **allotment** and singing.
feel: **Calm**, relieved to be left alone to do a job I'm good at.
S0.quote: Whatever the machines do for the owners, I want a fair share to reach the people who actually do the work.
fieldNote: Kira feels secure, with the mortgage gone and a steady household income, so the plateau barely moves her.
Her only worry is owners squeezing **bonuses**, which exists with or without AI.
She links work to fairness and union values, which shapes the quote.

steps.text: Keep using the chat tool to draft factory emails and translate specs
Carry on buying for spring and Christmas ranges as usual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that most of my job is going to change, and I'd rather be at the front of that than the back. I'd tell colleagues to stop pretending and start learning the tools. And I'd say to the owners, in the open, that nobody gets cut because software was bought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think around half my work, the price checks, the supplier comparisons, the reorder planning, goes to software within three years. What stays is judgement: which new product will sell, which factory will let us down. I'm fairly sure I can do that part, and I'm also fairly sure Brightwell will want to pay fewer people to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the vendor course on the new buying software this winter, and I'd use the chat tool every day on the comparisons. I'd ask my boss, Gail, to write down which tasks are mine and which are the machine's. And I'd stay in the union group so there's a record if hours are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit wobbly, but interested. I'm 58, so the clock matters, and I'd love to finish well rather than be eased out. It's more like standing at the edge of a cold swimming pool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two junior assistants, Priya and Mark. They do the data entry the software will take first. I'd try to teach them to check the software's work, because someone has to catch the daft mistakes, and I'd push to keep them on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask your boss Gail to write down which tasks are yours. What would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you'd have to build one. We make a list of what the software gets wrong each month, and show Gail. Software can compare prices all day, but somebody has to decide which new saucepan will actually sell in January.

say: I'd say my job will change, and I want to be at the **front**.
I'd tell the owners that nobody gets cut just because software was **bought**.
think: About half my work goes to **software** within three years.
What stays is **judgement**, but Brightwell may want to pay fewer people for it.
do: Sign up for the vendor **course** on the new buying software this winter.
Use the chat tool every day on **price** comparisons.
Ask my boss Gail to **write down** which tasks are mine and which the machine's.
feel: A bit **wobbly** but interested, like the edge of a cold swimming pool.
S1.quote: Software can compare prices all day, but somebody has to decide which new saucepan will actually sell in January.
fieldNote: Steady adapter: she moves early but carefully, with the union as a back-stop.
She reads the job as **judgement** against routine, and thinks about junior colleagues Priya and Mark.
Mood is uneasy because her own role looks safe but the team around her may shrink.

steps.text: Sign up for the vendor course on the new buying software
Ask Gail to write down which tasks are mine and which the machine's
Stay active in the staff union group so cuts get recorded

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless to let this land in two years with no plan. I'd say to the union and anyone listening that the government needs to put income support in place and make firms share what they save. I'd also say it online, a lot more bluntly than I normally do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is probably gone in two years. If AI can do any thinking job better and cheaper, a buyer is an obvious one. I might hold on a little longer because factory bosses like a person at the other end of the phone, but I wouldn't bet on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Brightwell for a deal to retire at 60, and I'd double the savings, keeping the money in simple funds. Joseph would stay on the buses for as long as it takes, because driving is safe for several years. I'd also help our daughter Abena, a nurse, move her savings into a deposit account, since nursing is hands-on and safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly, with a tight chest. I'm not scared of being poor, I'm scared of being useless after 36 years of being good at something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Kofi, in concrete terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son Kofi works in an office doing insurance claims, and that's thinking work. I'd tell him to start a trade course in the evenings, and I'd pay for it. I'd tell him it's not a punishment, it's insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry the owners might sell. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the owners may sell Brightwell to a bigger firm who'd replace us with software on day one. I'd push for a clause in any sale that guarantees pay for staff.

say: I'd say it's **reckless** to let this land in two years with no plan.
I'd demand **income support** and firms sharing their savings.
think: My buying job is probably **gone** in two years.
Factory bosses like a **person** on the phone, but I wouldn't bet on that.
do: Ask Brightwell for a deal to **retire** at 60.
Move savings into simple **funds** and a deposit account.
Pay for Kofi's evening **trade** course as insurance.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight chest, and afraid of being useless.
S2.quote: I'm not scared of being poor, I'm scared of being useless after 36 years of being good at something.
fieldNote: Money is not the fear; being **useless** after a long career is, and she says so without prompting.
Her thinking-work children, Kofi in claims and Abena in a hands-on job, shape her family plans.
She wants a sale clause guaranteeing staff pay, which links back to her union values.

steps.text: Ask Brightwell for a deal to retire at 60
Pay for Kofi's evening trade course
Push for a pay guarantee clause for staff if Brightwell is sold
Move savings into simple funds and a deposit account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say, is a gift if we use it. I'd tell friends that the time lets us push for laws on retraining and a shared fund. I'd say online that firms shouldn't wait for the last year to start planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd work for three more years and then see. I'd still be 63 when it arrives, so I'd probably have left. But I'm not at ease, because Joseph would still be working, and the bus companies are talking about self-driving buses, which come about three years after the thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 61 and then retire early if Brightwell offers it. I'd spend my last working years teaching Priya and Mark to check the machine's work, so they've got something to sell. I'd also start a modest side advisory thing for small shop owners, helping them choose what to stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. Five years is long enough to be sensible, and I'd feel like I have a plan. The worry for Joseph's job and our children stays at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Joseph's job. What would you ask him to do in these five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The self-driving buses, definitely. Joseph's depot has run trials already. I'd say to him: sign up for any upskilling the depot pays for, and take the fire-safety instructor course while it's on offer. That's the sort of ordinary thing that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the advisory work for small shops look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small shop owners drown in choice, so I'd help them pick fifty lines instead of five hundred, for a modest fee. And I'd want the union to plan with the bus company now.

say: I'd say five years is a **gift** if we use it for retraining.
I'd urge firms to start **planning** now, not in the last year.
think: I'd likely have **left** by then, but Joseph's bus job worries me.
Self-driving buses come about **three years** after the thinking AI.
do: Work until **61**, then retire early if Brightwell offers it.
Train **Priya** and Mark to check the software's work.
Start small **advisory** work helping shop owners choose stock.
feel: **Uneasy** but not frightened, with a plan and a worry for Joseph.
S3.quote: I'd spend my last working years teaching Priya and Mark to check the machine's work, so they've got something to sell.
fieldNote: With five years she sees time to act, so her mood stays uneasy rather than anxious.
Her concern shifts to her husband's bus job and the robot lag she's worked out herself.
The **advisory** idea is a realistic side income grounded in her buying skills.

steps.text: Work until 61, then retire early if Brightwell offers a deal
Train Priya and Mark to check the software's work
Start advisory work helping small shop owners choose stock

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent runway, and the argument should be about who benefits. I'd tell my friends to push their MPs for a shared dividend, and I'd say online that unions should be at the table now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my own job isn't touched, because I'm retired by 62 or 63. My worry is Abena and Kofi, who'd be in the middle of their careers when it arrives. I think about grandchildren too, we don't have any yet, but I hope for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on until 62 and then retire. I'd put some money into a fund for Kofi's retraining, and some towards Abena's house deposit. I'd also join a union retirees' group and a local group that talks about work and AI at the library.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm. It's far enough off that I'd rather enjoy the next few years and stay curious. I'd be a bit sad that the world I knew is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children now, if this were the picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids: stay curious and don't tie your whole identity to a job title. I did, for 36 years, and I liked it, but it's a little frightening to find out how much of me was Brightwell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel sad. Can you say more about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of grief, I think, for the factory calls and the whole rhythm of it. Ten years is a decent runway, but the real argument is about who gets the benefit when the machines do the thinking.

say: I'd say ten years is a decent **runway** and the argument is who benefits.
I'd urge friends to push MPs for a **shared dividend**.
think: My job isn't touched, but **Abena and Kofi** are mid-career when it lands.
I'm a little scared how much of me was **Brightwell**.
do: Put money into a fund for Kofi's **retraining** and Abena's deposit.
Join a union **retirees'** group and a library discussion group.
feel: Fairly **calm**, with some sadness that the world I knew is going.
S4.quote: Ten years is a decent runway, but the real argument is about who gets the benefit when the machines do the thinking.
fieldNote: At ten years her own work and money are secure, so she is calm and thinks about her children.
She admits how much of her identity was tied to the **job title**.
Politics and family plans, not job changes, dominate her actions.

steps.text: Carry on at Brightwell until 62, then retire
Put money into funds for Kofi's retraining and Abena's deposit
Join a union retirees' group and the library discussion group

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. Everything I'd do depends on time, and that one gives us none. What would help is an income guarantee, a share in the savings the firms make, and training paid for by someone other than the worker.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd say what I said at the beginning: I don't mind machines doing the thinking, but I want an honest share of the gain to reach the people who do the work. I keep coming back to fairness, because I think the machines can be good for people if the sharing is honest.

headlineQuote: I don't mind machines doing the thinking, but I want an honest share of the gain to reach the people who do the work.
portrait: Kira is **58**, a homeware buyer for Brightwell Home Supplies, who uses AI now and then and is willing to learn more.
She's progressive and union-minded, and often frames the AI question as one of **fairness** and who shares the gain.
Her mortgage is paid and her husband Joseph has a stable bus job, so she stays calm in mild worlds.
In the fast worlds she plans an early **retirement**, helps her children and pushes the union.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, with no time for support or fair sharing.
whatWouldHelp: An **income guarantee** and a share of savings, with training paid by someone other than workers.
